summary: This unit builds the everyday language and communication skills every tradesperson needs: listening and asking questions, speaking clearly, using body language well, taking and passing on phone messages, writing memos, letters, emails and reports in plain English, and reading workplace documents, labels and safety signs. You will also learn to spot and overcome barriers to communication, take part in meetings, give and receive feedback, and deal politely with complaints.

blocks.p: This unit is shared by several Level 2 programmes at the Centre: welding, electrical installation, cosmetology, beauty therapy and hospitality (villa and property services). The examples come from all of these trades. **Communication** is sharing information so that the other person understands it the way you meant it.

At work, poor communication costs time, money and sometimes safety: a gate made to the wrong width, the wrong hair colour mixed, a circuit switched on while someone is working on it, a guest left waiting because a message was never passed on. Good communication is a trade skill, just like welding, wiring or styling.

What this means at work

Give full attention, take notes, ask questions and say the message back to check it.
Speak clearly and ask good questions
Use plain words, a suitable tone, and open or closed questions; explain trade words.
Read and use eye contact, posture, facial expression and gestures; use agreed hand signals.
Spot noise, language, emotional and other barriers and deal with them.
Answer professionally, take and pass on messages, and calm an upset caller.
Write memos, letters, emails, notices, messages and incident reports in plain, correct English.
Skim and scan; follow instructions, labels, job cards and safety signs.
Work in meetings and handle feedback
Prepare, take part and follow up; give and receive feedback; deal with complaints politely.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the communication process, listening, speaking, body language, barriers, the telephone, writing, documents, signs, meetings and feedback.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms, abbreviations, punctuation, parts of speech, sign shapes and colours, 24-hour times) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two group practicals.** In the first, you role-play work phone calls: answer properly, take a message on a slip, read it back and pass it on, and give feedback on other members' calls. In the second, your group plans, drafts, checks and corrects a one-page staff notice, then each member presents part of it in a short briefing and answers a question.

blocks.note: Jamaican Creole (Patois) is a full language, and most Jamaicans use both it and English. At work, use clear Standard English in writing, on the phone, and with customers and visitors who may not understand Creole. Choosing the right language for the listener is a skill, not a put-down.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: The sender has an idea or information to share
The sender puts it into words, pictures or signs the receiver will understand
The sender chooses a channel: face to face, phone, text, email, memo, notice, sign or hand signal
The receiver gets the message and works out what it means
The receiver gives feedback: a reply, a question or an action that shows how the message was understood
If the feedback shows a mistake, the sender explains again

head: Part
Meaning
Example in a salon

"Leave the colour on for 30 minutes, then rinse with cool water."
The person who gets and understands the message
The reply or action that shows how the message was understood
"Thirty minutes, then a cool rinse. I'll set the timer."
Anything that stops the message getting through

Good for
Watch out for
rows: Quick instructions, showing how, sensitive matters; you can see the other person's reaction
No record; spoken details are easily forgotten
Quick questions and bookings when you cannot meet
No body language; names and numbers are easily misheard
Short updates, confirming times and addresses
Tone is easily misread; not for long or private matters; never while driving or using a machine
Replies can be slow; check the address before you send
The same message to all staff: rules, changes, reminders
Must be read to work; keep it short and clear
Warnings and instructions at the place they apply
Must be standard, in sight and kept clean
Noisy places, crane lifts, long distances
Only agreed signals; everyone must know them

head: Point
Spoken communication
Written communication
rows: Fast: the message goes at once and questions are answered straight away
Slower to prepare and to answer
None, unless someone writes it down
A lasting record that can be checked later
Tone of voice and body language help; you can check understanding at once
The same words reach many people; exact figures, sizes and dates stay exact
Quick instructions, warnings in an emergency, talking through a problem
Job cards, orders, incident reports, rule changes, and messages for someone who is not there

blocks.p: Often you use both: speak first, then confirm in writing. For example, agree a new delivery time with a customer by phone, then send a short message confirming the day and time.
Most mistakes at work begin with poor listening. **Active listening** means giving the speaker your full attention and checking that you have understood.

flow: Stop what you are doing, put your phone away and face the speaker
Deal with noise: move somewhere quieter, or wait until the machine is off
Show that you are listening: eye contact, nodding, short words such as "Yes" or "I see"; do not cut in
Note the key points: the job, sizes or amounts, the time it must be done by, the safety rules
Ask about anything you are not sure of
**Paraphrase**: say the main points back in your own words, so the speaker can correct any mistake

head: Signs of good listening
Signs of poor listening
rows: Questions and a summary at the end
Looking at a phone or the clock
Turning away to talk to someone else
Cutting in or finishing their sentences
Thinking about your reply instead of listening

blocks.p: Barriers to listening include machine noise, a phone in your hand, tiredness, worry or anger, and deciding what the speaker means before they have finished.

head: Type
What it does
Examples
rows: Invites a full answer; often starts with what, how, why or "tell me"
"How would you like the gate to open?" "What happened just before the breaker tripped?"
Gets a yes or no, or a single fact; quick to answer
"Is the client allergic to anything?" "Which room number?"
"Why do you think it overheated?" "Can you show me where it leaks?"
"So you want it ready by 3 p.m. on Friday, is that right?"

blocks.note: If you do not understand an instruction, ask until you do. Guessing wastes materials and time and can be dangerous. Nobody thinks less of a worker who asks a sensible question.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Think first: who is listening, what do they need to know, and what do you want them to do?
Speak clearly, at a steady pace, facing the listener.
Give the main point first, then the details, and keep to the point.
Use plain words, and explain any trade words.
Check that the listener has understood.

blocks.p: **Jargon** is the special trade words that outsiders may not know: undercut, polarity, GFCI, porosity, developer, cuticle, turndown service. Use them with co-workers who know them. With customers, explain them or use plain words instead. Instead of "Your GFCI tripped on a ground fault", say "The safety socket switched the power off because the kettle is leaking current. Please don't use the kettle until it has been checked."

Your tone shows your attitude as much as your words do. "Can I help you?" can sound warm and welcoming or bored and rude, depending on how you say it. Keep your tone calm, friendly and respectful, even when you are busy or the other person is upset. Avoid sarcasm and shouting.

blocks.h: Visitors and customers with little English

ul: Use short, simple words and short sentences.
Speak a little more slowly, not more loudly.
Avoid slang, Creole and trade words.
Point, show pictures or samples, and write numbers, times and prices down.
Check understanding, and be patient. A translation app can help, used with care.

blocks.p: For a briefing or a toolbox talk: plan your main points, stand where everyone can see and hear you, face them, speak clearly and loudly enough, keep to the point, use a picture or a sign if it helps, and finish by asking for questions.

blocks.h: Giving instructions to a new worker

flow: Explain what the job is and why it matters
Show how to do it
Let them do it while you watch
Ask them to tell you the key points back
Check on them again a little later

blocks.p: **Non-verbal communication** is the message we give without words: our face, eyes, hands, posture, the distance we stand at, and our appearance. People often notice body language first, and believe it more than words.

head: Good body language
Poor body language
rows: A friendly face and a smile
Looking away, at a phone or at the clock
Open posture: arms relaxed, facing the person

blocks.p: Reading body language: folded arms and a frown may mean someone is unhappy or does not agree. Ask gently rather than guess. Remember that customs differ: in some cultures people make less eye contact as a sign of respect.

In noisy places such as a welding shop, a crane lift, a plant room or a busy kitchen, spoken words may not be heard, so agreed **hand signals** are used. Learn the signals your workplace uses, use only those, make sure the other person has seen your signal, and stop if you are not sure. On a lift, a stop signal from anyone must be obeyed.
A **barrier** is anything that stops a message from being sent, received or understood correctly.

head: Barrier
Examples
How to overcome it
rows: Grinders, hair dryers, generators, a bad phone line, shouting across a site
Move somewhere quieter, wait until the machine stops, use hand signals, face the person
Different languages, strong accents, jargon, long words
Plain words; explain terms; show or draw it; check understanding
Anger, worry, tiredness, pain, not liking the speaker
Stay calm, choose a better time, let the person explain first
Different customs about eye contact, gestures and how to address people
Be respectful; use Mr, Mrs or Miss until invited to use a first name; ask politely
Too many links in the chain
A message passed on through several people
Give important messages directly, and in writing too; read them back
Untidy handwriting, unclear notes, poor eyesight
Print clearly, use a simple layout, read it aloud if needed
A flat phone battery, no signal, an email to the wrong address
Have a back-up; check addresses; confirm important messages

blocks.p: **The message chain.** A supervisor tells one worker, "Cut the 6 m tubes into 1.5 m lengths for the canopy." That worker tells a second, who tells a third. By the time it arrives it may be "Cut the tubes at 1.5 for the gate." Each link can change a detail or drop one. For anything about safety, sizes or times, go back to the person who gave the message.

blocks.note: After any important message, check understanding: ask the person to tell it back to you in their own words.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Answer within a few rings, with a pen and message pad ready
Greet the caller, then give the business name and your own name: "Good morning, [business name], Chevelle speaking. How can I help you?"
Listen; note the caller's name early and use it politely
Help, or explain that the person they want is not available and offer to take a message
Before the call ends, read the details back
Thank the caller and end the call politely

head: Write down
Why
rows: So it reaches the right person
The caller's full name, and company if any
So the person knows who to call; ask the caller to spell names
Read it back, in groups of digits, to check it
With the key facts: what, how many, what size, by when
Whether the caller wants a call back, and when
So the person knows what to do and how soon
The date and time of the call
So the person knows how old the message is
So the person can ask you about it

blocks.p: Pass the message on quickly: hand it over, or put it where the person will see it at once, and tell them if it is urgent.

ul: Let the caller explain without interrupting, and stay calm.
Do not argue, and do not take it personally.
Show that you understand: "I'm sorry you've had to wait, Mrs Henry."
Get the facts: name, number, job or booking details, what was promised.
Say what will happen next and when, and only promise what you can deliver.
Pass it to your supervisor if you cannot sort it out, and make sure someone follows up.
If a caller becomes abusive, stay polite and pass the call to your supervisor.
Ask before putting a caller on hold, and come back to them quickly.
When you transfer a call, tell the caller who you are putting them through to.
Never answer with "Yeah, who this?" or put the phone down on the desk and walk away.
Smile as you speak: it can be heard in your voice. Do not eat or chew while on the phone.
Keep personal calls for your breaks, and never use a phone while driving or working a machine.

blocks.p: Plain language is short, clear and easy to follow. It saves the reader's time and prevents mistakes.

head: Instead of
Write
rows: "Personnel are required to utilise the designated receptacles for the disposal of spent electrodes."
"Put used electrode stubs in the metal stub bin."
"In the event of the occurrence of a fire, evacuate the premises."
"If there is a fire, leave the building."
"Kindly be advised that the salon will not be operational on Monday."
"The salon will be closed on Monday."

ul: Keep sentences short, with one idea in each.
Put the main point first.
Say who does what: "Check the gas hose before use" is clearer than "The gas hose should be checked".
Write numbers, units, dates and times clearly: 1 200 mm, 15:30, Monday 8 March.
Check your writing before you send or hand it in.

head: Part of speech
What it does
Examples
rows: Names a person, place or thing
Says how, when or where something is done
Takes the place of a noun

head: Punctuation
Use
Example
rows: Separates items in a list, or parts of a sentence
Bring gloves, glasses and a face shield.
Starts a sentence and the names of people, places, days and months
Mrs Reid will call on Monday.
Shows who owns something, or a missing letter
A strong warning or feeling; use sparingly at work

head: Abbreviation
Meaning
rows: reference (for example a job or invoice number)

blocks.p: A **memo** (memorandum) is a short written message sent inside a workplace. It starts with a heading block, then gives the main point first, the reason, what staff must do, and who to contact.

head: Part
Example
rows: New laundry collection time from Monday 8 March

From Monday 8 March the laundry van will collect used linen at 10:30, not 14:00. Please have all bags tagged and at the side gate by 10:15. The change means clean linen comes back the same day. If you have any questions, please see me in the office.

ul: Your business's address and the date at the top, then the name and address of the person you are writing to.
If you know the person's name, begin "Dear Mr Morrison," and end "Yours sincerely,".
If you do not know the name, begin "Dear Sir or Madam," and end "Yours faithfully,".
A subject line, then short paragraphs: why you are writing, the details, and what happens next.
Your signature, your printed name and your job title.
Never "Hey", "Yo" or slang in a letter to a customer.

head: Part
Use
rows: People who should see the email for information; everyone can see who was copied
People who get a copy without the other receivers seeing their address
A short summary of what the email is about, for example "Quote for 4 window grills, 14 Palm Avenue"
A polite greeting, the main point first, short paragraphs
A clearly named file; check that it is attached before you send
Your name, job title, business and phone number

ul: Check the address, spelling, figures and attachment before you press send.
Do not write whole words in capitals: it reads as shouting.
Do not forward private information without permission, and reply promptly.

blocks.p: An **incident report** records an accident or a near miss. It records facts, not blame or opinions, and it is written as soon as possible, while you remember clearly.

head: Include
Example
rows: "Mr Powell tripped over a welding lead lying across the walkway and fell onto his left knee."
"The walkway beside Bay 2 in the fabrication workshop."
Who was involved, and who saw it
"Graze and swelling on the left knee; cleaned and dressed by the first aider, Mr Daley."
"Lead re-routed along the wall; walkway checked; supervisor informed."
Your name, signature and the date

blocks.note: Write what you saw and did, in the order it happened. Do not guess, blame people or give opinions about their attitude, and do not leave out facts that make you look bad. A false or incomplete report can let the same accident happen again.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Read it through slowly, aloud if you can.
Check spelling with a dictionary or a spell-checker, but read it yourself too: a spell-checker will not notice "there" written for "their".
Check every fact, name, number, date and time.
Ask yourself: will the reader know exactly what to do?

sections.title: Reading at work: documents, labels and signs

head: Skill
What you do
Use it when
rows: Read quickly through a text to get the general idea, using headings and first lines
Deciding whether a memo affects you; getting the gist of a manual
Look quickly down a page for one fact, guided by headings and key words
Finding a phone number, a size on a drawing, a mixing time on a label
Read every word carefully, more than once if needed
Safety instructions, a procedure you will follow, anything you sign

head: Document
What it is for
rows: What the customer wants: the work to be done, materials and the date
The hours you worked on each job; it must be true and accurate
What has been delivered; check it against the goods before you sign
What is being ordered from a supplier
A bill asking the customer to pay
A phone message for someone who was not there
How to use, mix, store and maintain a product or machine safely
The hazards of a chemical, safe handling and storage, the PPE to wear, first aid and what to do with spills

blocks.p: Before you use any new product (a cleaning chemical, a hair colour, a solvent, a gas, an electrode), read its label and the maker's instructions: what it is, how to use or mix it, the PPE to wear, the hazards, first aid and storage. If anything is unclear, ask before you use it. Trades also read drawings, wiring diagrams and charts: check the title, the units, the scale and the date or revision, and ask if anything is unclear.

head: Type
Shape and colours
Meaning
Examples
rows: Red circle with a red diagonal bar, on white, black symbol
No smoking; no naked flames; do not touch
Blue circle with a white symbol
Wear eye protection; wear gloves; wear ear protection
Yellow triangle with a black border and black symbol
Green square or rectangle with a white symbol
The safe way, or safety equipment
Emergency exit (running figure and arrow); first aid; eye wash
Red square or rectangle with a white symbol
Fire extinguisher; fire alarm call point; fire hose

blocks.note: Signs work only if they are seen and obeyed. Report a sign that is missing, damaged or hidden behind stock.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The list of topics to be discussed, in order, sent out before the meeting
The person who leads the meeting and keeps it to the agenda and the time
The written record of what was discussed and agreed, and who will do what by when
A task given to a named person, with a deadline
The last item, for short points that are not on the agenda

head: When
What you do
rows: Read the agenda and think about each topic
Prepare any facts, figures or ideas you want to raise
Arrive on time with a pen and notebook
Listen, and wait your turn to speak
Speak clearly and keep to the topic
Respect other views, even when you disagree
Note the decisions and any task given to you
Do your tasks by the agreed date
Tell the person in charge when each task is done, or if there is a problem

blocks.p: A **toolbox talk** is a short meeting at the start of a shift about the day's work and its hazards. Arrive on time, listen, ask questions and sign the attendance sheet.

ul: Take turns, and do not speak over other people.
Listen, and respect other views.
Disagree politely: "I see your point, but I think ..."
Stay on the topic.
Share your ideas: staying silent helps nobody.
Be specific: "The bead on the second joint is uneven at the start" helps; "Your welding is bad" does not.
Talk about the work, not the person, and give feedback in private where you can.
Start with what was done well, then say how to improve.
Be polite, and check that the person understood.
Listen without arguing or making excuses.
Do not take it personally: it is about the work.
Ask questions: "How should I do it?"
Thank the person, act on it and correct the work.
Never blame a co-worker for your own mistake.

flow: Stay calm and polite, and give the customer your full attention
Let them explain the whole problem without cutting in
Show that you understand and thank them for telling you; do not argue or blame a co-worker
Ask questions and write down the facts: name, job number, the date promised, what is wrong
Say clearly what will happen next and when; if you cannot fix it, pass it to your supervisor and say when the customer will hear back
Follow up, and make sure it was done

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it.

ul: I can name the parts of the communication process: sender, message, channel, receiver and feedback.
I can choose the best channel for a message, and say when spoken or written communication is better.
I can listen actively, take notes and paraphrase to check my understanding.
I can ask open, closed, probing and checking questions.
I can speak clearly, avoid or explain jargon, and use a suitable tone.
I can speak simply and patiently to a visitor with little English.
I can read and use body language, and I know why agreed hand signals are used.
I can name barriers to communication and say how to overcome each one.
I can answer a work phone professionally, take a complete message and pass it on.
I can deal calmly with an upset caller or a customer's complaint.
I can write in plain English, using nouns, verbs, punctuation and common abbreviations correctly.
I can set out a memo, a formal letter and an email, and I know what To, CC, BCC and Subject are for.
I can write a factual incident report.
I can skim and scan, and read job cards, time sheets, labels and safety data sheets.
I can tell the five kinds of safety sign by shape and colour.
I can prepare for, take part in and follow up a meeting.
I can give and receive feedback in a helpful way.

c1.title: A gate enquiry by phone in Half Way Tree
c1.text: Chevelle works in the office of a small fabrication shop in Half Way Tree, Kingston. At 2:20 p.m. on Tuesday, a caller, Mr Desmond Wright, asks for the owner, Mr Ellis, who is out on site until 4:00 p.m. Mr Wright wants a quote for a sliding gate 4.5 metres wide and wants Mr Ellis to call him back today on 876-555-0142. A grinder is running in the next room.

c2.title: A toolbox talk on a site in Junction
c2.text: Rushane, a new electrical apprentice, has joined a team wiring a supermarket in Junction, St Elizabeth. The foreman, Mr Clarke, gives the toolbox talk at 7:00 a.m. beside a running concrete mixer. He says the main panel will be energised at 2:00 p.m. and that nobody is to work on the lighting circuits after that without his permission. Rushane arrives late and hears the message from another apprentice, who heard it from a carpenter.

c3.title: A visitor at a nail studio in Negril
c3.text: Jodian works the nail desk at a small spa in Negril, Westmoreland. Mrs Weber, a visitor from Germany, speaks only a little English. She points to a photo of nail art and asks, "How long? How much?" It is the end of a long day, Jodian is tired, and a colleague is playing loud music nearby.

c4.title: A fall at a villa in Runaway Bay
c4.text: At 10:40 a.m. on Friday 12 March, at a villa in Runaway Bay, St Ann, the gardener, Mr Lewis, slipped on the patio, which Kadeen, a housekeeper, had just mopped, and hurt his wrist. Kadeen saw him fall. She had not put out a wet-floor sign. The manager, Mrs Francis, gave first aid and drove Mr Lewis to the clinic. She asks Kadeen to write an incident report and email it to her, with a copy to the villa's owner.

c5.title: Signs and labels in a workshop in Black River
c5.text: Tamoya is a trainee at the Centre's workshop in Black River, St Elizabeth. Her instructor gives her a new degreasing spray to clean steel before painting and asks her to find, from its 12-page safety data sheet (SDS), which gloves to wear. The paint cupboard carries a yellow triangle with a black flame, and the workshop has an eye-wash station.

c6.title: A staff meeting at a salon in Spaldings
c6.text: Miss Hutchinson, who owns a salon in Spaldings, Clarendon, has sent out an agenda for a 30-minute staff meeting on Thursday at 8:00 a.m.: a new booking system, towel laundering, and the Christmas rota. Nickeisha, a junior stylist, has an idea for cutting clients' waiting times that fits the booking-system item.

questions.q: The grinder makes it hard for Chevelle to hear Mr Wright. What should she do?
o: Guess the words she misses and check them with Mr Ellis later
Ask him to hold briefly, close the door or move, then carry on
Ask Mr Wright to speak up so she can hear him over the noise
Hang up and wait for him to call back when it is quieter
questions.why: Noise is a physical barrier. Dealing with it first, with the caller's agreement, means she can hear the name, number and details correctly; guessing leads to wrong messages.

questions.q: Which message slip is the most useful for Mr Ellis?
o: Tuesday afternoon. Mr Wright rang about a big gate, sounded keen. Please call him back when you can. Chevelle
Desmond Wright, 876-555-0142, wants a gate made for his house. Call him back some time. Taken by Chevelle, Tuesday
2:20 p.m. A customer on 876-555-0142 wants a quote for a sliding gate, 4.5 m wide, today. Chevelle
Tue 2:20 p.m. Desmond Wright, 876-555-0142: quote for a 4.5 m sliding gate; call back today. Chevelle
questions.why: A good slip has the caller's full name and number, the message with its key facts (a quote for a 4.5 m sliding gate), when to call back, the date and time, and who took it. Each of the others leaves out the number, the name, the size or the "today".

questions.q: Mr Wright says his surname quickly. Chevelle is not sure whether it is "Wright", "Right" or "Rite". What should she do?
o: Ask him to spell it, then read it back to him
Write "Right", the spelling that seems most likely
Leave the surname off and write only "Desmond"
Write all three spellings so Mr Ellis can choose
questions.why: Names are easily misheard, and a wrong spelling makes the customer hard to find in the records and can make him feel unvalued. Asking him to spell it and reading it back is quick and professional.

questions.q: At 4:15 p.m. Mr Ellis is still out, and Mr Wright calls again, annoyed that nobody has called him. What should Chevelle say first?
o: "Mr Ellis is very busy on site, so you will have to wait like everyone else."
"It isn't my fault. I wrote your message down and left it on his desk."
"I'm sorry nobody has called you, Mr Wright. Let me find out why."
"Please don't raise your voice, sir, or I will have to end this call now."
questions.why: An upset caller first needs to feel heard: apologise for the delay, stay calm and blame nobody. Then find out what is happening, by reaching Mr Ellis, and tell the caller honestly when he will get his call.

questions.q: Rushane got the energising message through two other people. What should he do?
o: Ask Mr Clarke himself to confirm the time and the circuits
Trust the apprentice's version, as safety messages are simple
Carry on with the lighting circuits until someone stops him
Ask the carpenter to repeat it more slowly, word for word
questions.why: A message passed on through two people may have lost or changed details, such as the time or which circuits. For anything about safety, go to the person who gave the message and confirm it, and arrive on time for toolbox talks.

questions.q: Which barrier did Mr Clarke create by where he gave the talk?
o: Language: trade words the team did not know
Physical: the noise of the running mixer
Emotional: the team being upset about the work
Cultural: different ideas about eye contact
questions.why: Noise is a physical barrier: people miss words and often do not like to say so. Giving the talk away from the mixer, or stopping it for a few minutes, removes the barrier.

questions.q: Later Mr Clarke tells Rushane, "Run a 20 A circuit to the cold room and land it on breaker 14." Rushane is not sure what "land it" means. Which reply is best?
o: "No problem, sir, I'll work out what you mean when I get there."
"Why do you use words that a new apprentice can't understand?"
"Could someone else do that one? I'm not sure about breakers."
"Sorry, sir, by 'land it' do you mean connect it to breaker 14?"
questions.why: A checking question in his own words lets Mr Clarke confirm or correct him before he starts. Guessing, complaining about the jargon or passing the job on all avoid the problem instead of solving it.

questions.q: Which is the best way for Jodian to answer Mrs Weber?
o: Speak louder and faster so that the explanation is over quickly
Use the proper trade names for each step so she trusts the work
Speak slowly in short, simple words, and write the time and price
Switch to Creole, since visitors like to hear the local language
questions.why: With a visitor who has little English, use short, plain words, a slower pace, and pictures, pointing and written numbers. Volume, speed, jargon and Creole all make it harder for her to understand.

questions.q: While Mrs Weber is choosing, Jodian leans on the desk with her arms folded and keeps glancing at the clock. What is Mrs Weber most likely to think?
o: That Jodian is relaxed and friendly with guests
That Jodian is not interested in serving her
That the spa is about to give her a discount
That Jodian is listening closely to her needs
questions.why: Body language often speaks louder than words, and a visitor who shares little language relies on it even more. Folded arms and clock-watching suggest boredom or impatience; standing up, smiling and making eye contact show welcome.

questions.q: What should Jodian do about the loud music before she explains the treatment?
o: Ask her colleague politely to turn it down while she serves
Raise her voice above the music so that the guest can hear
Explain everything in writing so the music makes no difference
Ignore it, as guests expect a lively feel at a beach spa
questions.why: Loud music is a physical barrier, and removing it is easier than shouting over it, especially for a guest who is working hard to follow English. Writing the price down helps too, but not instead of talking with her.

questions.q: Which sentence belongs in Kadeen's incident report?
o: "Mr Lewis is always in a hurry and never looks where he is going."
"The fall was probably the gardener's fault, not housekeeping's."
"I think Mrs Francis should have bought anti-slip tiles long ago."
"At 10:40 a.m. Mr Lewis slipped on the wet patio and held his wrist."
questions.why: An incident report records facts: what happened, where, when, who was involved and what was done. Opinions and blame do not help to prevent the next accident and can be unfair.

questions.q: Kadeen did not put out a wet-floor sign. What should her report say about this?
o: State it plainly as a fact, with when she mopped
Leave it out, since nobody has asked her about the sign
Say a sign was put out but the gardener did not read it
Say that wet-floor signs are not needed on an open patio
questions.why: A report must be honest and complete, even when a fact is uncomfortable. The missing sign is a cause that can be put right; hiding it lets the accident happen again, and a false report is serious misconduct.

questions.q: Where should Kadeen put the villa owner's email address?
o: In the To box, in place of Mrs Francis's address
In the BCC box, so Mrs Francis cannot see it was sent
In the CC box, as the owner needs a copy for information
In the Subject line, so that the owner sees it first
questions.why: The To box is for the main receiver, Mrs Francis. CC sends a copy to someone who should see the message for information, and everyone can see who was copied; BCC would hide the copy from Mrs Francis.

questions.q: Which subject line is best for Kadeen's email?
o: Very important, please read as soon as possible, thanks
Incident report: patio fall, Mr Lewis, Friday 12 March
Hi Mrs Francis, here is the report you asked me for
Accident!!! Gardener hurt badly on patio, please call
questions.why: A subject line says briefly and exactly what the email is about, so that it can be found and dealt with. Vague or alarming subjects and strings of exclamation marks are not professional.

questions.q: Tamoya needs the eye-wash station quickly. Which kind of sign should she look for?
o: A blue circle with a white symbol
A yellow triangle with a black symbol
A red circle with a diagonal bar
A green square with a white symbol
questions.why: Green signs show safe conditions: first aid, eye wash, emergency exits and escape routes. Blue circles are orders (you must), yellow triangles warn of hazards, and red circles with a bar forbid something.

questions.q: Tamoya wants to grind some steel right next to the paint cupboard with the flame warning sign. What should she do?
o: Grind well away, as sparks could set the contents alight
Carry on, since the sign only matters when the door is open
Carry on, but stand a fire extinguisher on top of the cupboard
Put tape over the sign so that visitors are not worried by it
questions.why: A yellow triangle with a flame warns that flammable materials are stored there. Grinding sparks can travel several metres and start a fire, so the work moves well away; an extinguisher nearby is not a substitute for distance.

questions.q: Which reading skill will find the right gloves fastest on the 12-page SDS?
o: Skimming: read the whole sheet quickly for the general idea
Scanning: look down the headings for protective equipment
Close reading: read every page slowly from the beginning
Proofreading: check the sheet for any spelling mistakes
questions.why: Scanning means looking quickly for one fact, guided by headings and key words; on an SDS, protective equipment has its own section. Skimming gives the general idea, and close reading is for steps she must follow, such as first aid.

questions.q: What should Nickeisha do before the meeting?
o: Wait to hear what the others say before thinking about it
Read the agenda and jot down her idea with a short example
Tell a senior stylist her idea so that she raises it instead
Plan to raise it right at the start, before the first item
questions.why: Preparing means reading the agenda, thinking about each item and noting what she wants to say, so that she can put her idea clearly at the right point in the meeting.

questions.q: During the meeting, a senior stylist says of Nickeisha's idea, "That will never work here." What is the best response?
o: Stay silent for the rest of the meeting to avoid an argument
Tell the stylist that her own ideas are old-fashioned
Leave the meeting early, since the decision has been made
Ask calmly which part would not work, and explain her idea
questions.why: In a discussion, disagree politely and keep to the topic. Asking what the problem is shows respect for the other view and gives her the chance to explain; silence, insults or walking out help nobody.

questions.q: After the meeting, Miss Hutchinson tells Nickeisha, "Your idea was good, but you spoke over two people." What is the best reaction?
o: Thank her, and plan to wait her turn at the next meeting
Explain that the others were too slow to make their points
Agree, but tell the others it was the senior stylist's fault
Say nothing, and stop putting forward ideas at meetings
questions.why: Feedback is about the work, not the person. Listening, thanking the person and acting on it is the professional response; excuses, blame or sulking stop you improving.
